newsitem.title: UK: British ministers lose right to royal venison.
newsitem.headline: British ministers lose right to royal venison.

text.p: Senior British ministers have lost their right to receive haunches of venison twice a year from royal deer parks under a warrant which dates back to 1100.
A spokeswoman at the Culture Department said on Monday the government had decided the perks were "an inappropriate use of taxpayers' money".

The gifts, worth some 450 pounds ($720) a year, have been claimed by around 100 ministers, senior civil servants and members of the royal household. They pay only a nominal charge towards the cost of transporting the meat.
The spokeswoman said over the years the list of people on the Warrant had grown so that it was dominated by politicians and senior civil servants.
"It has been decided to return the warrant to its original form under which the gifts went to the closest friends and advisers of the monarch," she said.

Venison from the annual deer cull in the Royal Parks at Richmond and Hampton Court in south-west London and in the New Forest in southern England which had been used to supply ministers and civil servants will instead be marketed commercially, she said.
The custom of giving venison to Royal aides dates from the reign of Henry the First, son of William the Conqueror, the Norman who invaded England in 1066.
